Content:
In a previous lesson, we discussed that there are two main types of automata: acceptors and transducers. Recall:

Content:
- An acceptor is a machine that receives a string as input and then either accepts or rejects the string.
- A transducer is a machine that receives a string as input and then returns another string as output.

Content:
In this lesson, we will focus on transducers.

Content:
One example of a transducer is the Mealy machine, which processes an input string and produces a corresponding output string.

Content:
More formally, a Mealy machine is a six-tuple of the form [MATH: M=(Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, \omega, q_0),] where:

Content:
- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states. These are all the possible configurations the machine can be in.
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols. The machine can process this "alphabet" of symbols as inputs.
- [MATH: \Gamma] is a nonempty finite set of output symbols. The machine can write this "alphabet" of symbols as outputs.
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q.] It takes a state and an input symbol and returns a state. This function determines how the machine moves from one state to another based on a given input symbol.
- [MATH: \omega] is an output function of the form [MATH: \omega : Q \times \Sigma \to \Gamma.] It takes a state and an input symbol and returns an output symbol. This function determines what symbol to write based on a given state and input symbol.
- [MATH: q_0 \in Q] is a start state (or initial state). This is the state in which the machine begins.

Content:
We can visualize a Mealy machine as a directed graph where

Content:
- the vertices represent the states,
- the arcs, labeled with input and output symbols, represent transitions from one state to another, and the corresponding output symbol, and
- the start state is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In a previous lesson, we discussed that there are two main types of automata: acceptors and transducers. Recall:

Content:
- An acceptor is a machine that receives a string as input and then either accepts or rejects the string.
- A transducer is a machine that receives a string as input and then returns another string as output.

Content:
In this lesson, we will focus on transducers.

Content:
One example of a transducer is the Mealy machine, which processes an input string and produces a corresponding output string.

Content:
More formally, a Mealy machine is a six-tuple of the form [MATH: M=(Q, \Sigma, \Gamma, \delta, \omega, q_0),] where:

Content:
- [MATH: Q] is a nonempty finite set of states. These are all the possible configurations the machine can be in.
- [MATH: \Sigma] is a nonempty finite set of input symbols. The machine can process this "alphabet" of symbols as inputs.
- [MATH: \Gamma] is a nonempty finite set of output symbols. The machine can write this "alphabet" of symbols as outputs.
- [MATH: \delta] is a transition function of the form [MATH: \delta : Q \times \Sigma \to Q.] It takes a state and an input symbol and returns a state. This function determines how the machine moves from one state to another based on a given input symbol.
- [MATH: \omega] is an output function of the form [MATH: \omega : Q \times \Sigma \to \Gamma.] It takes a state and an input symbol and returns an output symbol. This function determines what symbol to write based on a given state and input symbol.
- [MATH: q_0 \in Q] is a start state (or initial state). This is the state in which the machine begins.

Content:
We can visualize a Mealy machine as a directed graph where

Content:
- the vertices represent the states,
- the arcs, labeled with input and output symbols, represent transitions from one state to another, and the corresponding output symbol, and
- the start state is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to.]

Content:
An example of a Mealy machine is shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/37da554bcf0b2cadcc858d97ce976413]

Content:
In this case, the machine has the following components:

Content:
- The set of states [MATH: Q = \{p,q,r\}] (represented by the vertices).
- The set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma = \{0,1\}] (represented by the first part of the arcs' labels).
- The set of output symbols [MATH: \Gamma = \{0,1\}] (represented by the second part of the arcs' labels).
- The transition and output functions [MATH: \delta] and [MATH: \omega] with the following transitions and outputs defined by the arcs:
[MATH: δ(p, 0)|= r,|δ(p, 1)|= q,|ω(p, 0)|= 1,|ω(p, 1)|= 0,; δ(q, 0)|= p,|δ(q, 1)|= r,|ω(q, 0)|= 0,|ω(q, 1)|= 0,; δ(r, 0)|= q,|δ(r, 1)|= r|ω(r, 0)|= 1,|ω(r, 1)|= 1]
For instance, the arrow from [MATH: p] to [MATH: q,] labeled [MATH: 1/0,] means that [MATH: \delta(p,1) = q] and [MATH: \omega(p,1) = 0.]

[IMG: /graphics/29e0d7b1dd47640ee59d76dca698b1f2]
- The start state [MATH: p] (that is labeled by the input arrow [MATH: \to]), as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/a08878928cff68594887a5dbd95ab4c3]

Item 2 — Tutorial: Transition and Output Tables of Mealy Machines

Content:
Transition and output functions, [MATH: \delta] and [MATH: \omega,] are often put into tables, where a row represents a state [MATH: q,] a column represents an input symbol [MATH: a,] and their intersection is the value of the functions [MATH: \delta(q,a)] and [MATH: \omega(q,a),] respectively.

Below is an example of a Mealy machine's transition table (on the left) and output table (on the right). Note that we place [MATH: \to] next to the start state in the transition table.

- the set of input symbols [MATH: \Sigma = \{0,1\}] (given by the columns),
- the set of output symbols [MATH: \Gamma = \{x,y\}] (given by the values in the output table),
- the start state [MATH: p] (labeled by [MATH: \to] in the transition table), and
- the transition function [MATH: \delta] and the output function [MATH: \omega] are given in the tables.
